items.label: f02-optimistic-triple
items.front: What are the three moments of an optimistic mutation in TanStack Query, and what does each do?
items.back: onMutate: cancel in-flight refetches, SNAPSHOT the cache, apply the optimistic change, return the snapshot. onError: restore the snapshot. onSettled: invalidate so server truth (real ids, recomputed totals) replaces the guess - even on success.

items.label: f01-why-view-model
items.front: Name four ways a raw Prisma row leaks into the UI if the service does not map it to a view-model.
items.back: Decimal/raw cents the UI might do float math on; nullable joins (images: []) every call site must defend; _count aggregate objects instead of a plain productCount; and column/relation names that become an implicit API, so renames or ORM swaps turn into UI changes.

items.label: f03-integer-cents
items.front: ADR-0002 rejected two alternatives to branded integer cents. Which, and why?
items.back: Float dollars (19.99): invisible accumulation error. A big-decimal library: real but heavier than a single-currency shop needs, and it hides the lesson. Also rejected: unbranded number cents, which loses the compile-time guard.

items.prompt: A product has three variants that all cost 2500 cents. How does its card price read?

choices.text: No price until a variant is picked
A flat $25.00
From $25.00

choices: No price until a variant is picked
A flat $25.00

items.explanation: priceVaries is new Set(variants.map(v => v.priceCents)).size > 1 - a multi-variant product whose variants share a price is not a range. 'From $X' is a service decision.

items.prompt: Where does a cents value become a human-readable string in Storefront?

In the service view-model, next to the integer cents
In the repository, so the database returns formatted strings
Only in formatMoney, at the display edge

In the repository, so the database returns formatted strings
Only in formatMoney, at the display edge

items.explanation: Do all arithmetic on the integer; convert to a display string exactly once, at the edge.

items.prompt: A Server Component needs the product list. Why should it call listProducts() directly instead of fetch("/api/products")?

choices.text: Route handlers cannot be cached, but service functions can be
fetch is unavailable inside Server Components in the App Router
Calling the service directly bypasses the API's authentication checks
It is already on the server; fetching itself is a needless round-trip

choices: Route handlers cannot be cached, but service functions can be
fetch is unavailable inside Server Components in the App Router
Calling the service directly bypasses the API's authentication checks
It is already on the server; fetching itself is a needless round-trip

items.explanation: Server Components can await data through services; the API route exists for clients, not for the server's own rendering.

items.prompt: An order-level discount of 1000 cents is split across 3 equal lines with allocate(money(1000), [1,1,1]). What are the shares?

choices.text: 333.33 each

choices: 333.33 each

items.explanation: Largest-remainder allocation floors each share, then hands the leftover cent to the largest remainder, so the parts sum to exactly 1000 and line totals add up to what the customer paid.

items.prompt: A Client Component accidentally imports listProducts from server/services/catalog.ts. What stops this from shipping?

choices.text: The Prisma client throws at runtime when executed in the browser
Nothing; Next.js tree-shakes server code out of client bundles
TypeScript rejects async functions inside client component files
import "server-only" in the service makes the build fail

choices: The Prisma client throws at runtime when executed in the browser
Nothing; Next.js tree-shakes server code out of client bundles
TypeScript rejects async functions inside client component files
import "server-only" in the service makes the build fail

items.explanation: server-only is one of two guards on the seam; the ESLint layering rule (components may not import server/data, services may not import next/*, React or Prisma) is the other.

items.prompt: A product has two images and neither is flagged isPrimary. What image does the view-model carry?

choices.text: null
The first image
A generated placeholder URL
Both images

choices: null
The first image
A generated placeholder URL
Both images

items.explanation: find(isPrimary) ?? images[0] ?? null - only a product with no images at all gets null; the nullable join becomes an explicit null at the boundary so call sites do not each defend against images: [].

items.prompt: An optimistic add-to-cart applies the new line in onMutate but wires no onError rollback (and no invalidating onSettled). The server answers 409 (out of stock). What does the shopper see?

choices.text: The item disappears at once because the mutation failed
A phantom item that stays until a hard refresh
A toast appears and the item is removed automatically
TanStack Query restores the previous cache on any error

choices: The item disappears at once because the mutation failed
A phantom item that stays until a hard refresh
A toast appears and the item is removed automatically
TanStack Query restores the previous cache on any error

items.explanation: Snapshot in onMutate, restore in onError, reconcile in onSettled - a mutation with onMutate but no onError is an incomplete diff. It is not a rare edge case - it is every failed mutation.

choices.text: The ESLint layering rule forbids JSON columns in view-models
No S02 screen renders them, and the DTO grows only on demand
They were forgotten, and a later sprint flags the omission as a bug
Attributes are too large to serialize across the RSC boundary

choices: The ESLint layering rule forbids JSON columns in view-models
No S02 screen renders them, and the DTO grows only on demand
They were forgotten, and a later sprint flags the omission as a bug
Attributes are too large to serialize across the RSC boundary

items.explanation: ADR-0003: map to a view-model at the service, but don't pre-map fields no screen uses yet - S03's variant picker is the first consumer.

choices.text: It stores 164.9175, and formatMoney rounds it for display
It silently rounds 164.9175 to 165 cents inside the money() constructor
money() throws on the non-integer; round the rate multiply once, upstream
TypeScript rejects the call at compile time because the argument is not Cents

choices: It stores 164.9175, and formatMoney rounds it for display
It silently rounds 164.9175 to 165 cents inside the money() constructor
money() throws on the non-integer; round the rate multiply once, upstream

items.explanation: The constructor's throw is the guardrail: if you see it, something upstream did float math. The rate multiply is the one unavoidable rounding - do it once, deliberately.

choices.text: The whole page subtree joins the client bundle
The page can no longer be rendered on the server at all
None: the directive only affects that one file's own code
Server data stops flowing as props, so the page renders empty

choices: The whole page subtree joins the client bundle
The page can no longer be rendered on the server at all
None: the directive only affects that one file's own code
Server data stops flowing as props, so the page renders empty

items.explanation: Push "use client" down: mark the button or picker, not the page. Server Components ship no JS for themselves.

items.prompt: Why is Cents a branded number type rather than a plain number of cents?

choices.text: Because Prisma requires branded types when mapping Int columns
So that JSON serialization emits every cents value as a string
So a raw number cannot pose as Cents without going through money()
Branding changes the runtime representation to a 64-bit integer

choices: Because Prisma requires branded types when mapping Int columns
So that JSON serialization emits every cents value as a string
So a raw number cannot pose as Cents without going through money()
Branding changes the runtime representation to a 64-bit integer

items.explanation: At runtime Cents is a number; at compile time const price: Cents = 1999 will not compile - a nearly free guard against dollars or bare arithmetic results posing as money.
